figures.caption: The preparation of lead(II)sulfate by precipitation from two soluble salts

specPoints.text: describe an experiment to prepare a pure, dry sample of an insoluble salt, starting from two soluble reactants
practical: prepare a sample of pure, dry lead(II) sulfate

primer.text: From Prepare an Insoluble Salt you already know the precipitation pattern of two soluble salts swapping partners. This note runs that pattern as a named practical, with measured volumes, filtration, washing and drying, ending with a dry sample of lead(II) sulfate.

lessons.title: Aim
lessons.opening: This practical prepares a dry sample of lead(II) sulfate, an insoluble salt, from two solutions that are both soluble. Lead(II) nitrate provides the lead ions and potassium sulfate provides the sulfate ions, and when the two solutions meet, white lead(II) sulfate falls out of the mixture while potassium nitrate stays behind in the liquid.
keyPoints: The aim is a pure, dry sample of lead(II) sulfate.
The reactants are lead(II) nitrate solution and potassium sulfate solution.
Both reactants must be soluble while the product must be insoluble.
Lead(II) sulfate forms as the precipitate.
Potassium nitrate remains dissolved in the liquid above the solid.

low.restatement: Two clear solutions, lead(II) nitrate and potassium sulfate, are mixed, and white lead(II) sulfate drops out as a solid. The potassium nitrate made alongside it stays dissolved, so the solid can be filtered off as the product.
low.analogy: It is like two crowds meeting in a doorway where only one pairing is incompatible: the incompatible pair, lead and sulfate, clumps together and steps aside as a solid.
low.examPointer: State both reactant solutions by name and the white precipitate by name, because the practical mark scheme expects the full cast, not just the product.

medium.restatement: The ionic story is that Pb2+ meets SO42- and their insoluble compound leaves the solution, while the spectator ions K+ and NO3- never leave it. The design constraint is the same as any precipitation: both chosen reactants must dissolve so they can meet, and the chosen product must not dissolve so it can be collected.
medium.analogy: The spectator ions are like the audience at a match: they are present for every moment of it but never step onto the pitch, which belongs only to the lead and sulfate players.
medium.examPointer: Ionic-equation questions want Pb2+ plus SO42- giving PbSO4, with the spectator ions left out entirely.

check.stem: Which two solutions are mixed in this practical?

options.explanation: Those are the two soluble salts named by the practical.
Those are the products, not the starting solutions.
Lead(II) chloride is insoluble and is not the named reactant.
That is a different reaction family altogether; no metal is used here.

check.stem: Why must both starting solutions be soluble?

options.text: So they can be mixed as solutions and react in water
options.explanation: Ions can only meet in solution, which requires both reactants to dissolve.
Toxicity is a separate issue here; the constraint is about meeting in solution.
The rate is not the issue; the ability to form solutions is.
The product must stay insoluble for the method to collect it.

check.stem: What happens to the potassium nitrate formed?

options.text: It stays dissolved in the liquid and is washed away later
options.explanation: As a soluble salt it never leaves solution, and the wash carries its traces off the solid.

options.text: It precipitates alongside the lead(II) sulfate
options.explanation: Only the insoluble salt precipitates; potassium nitrate is soluble.
A dissolved salt cannot evaporate with the water; it stays until the wash.

options.text: It turns into more lead(II) sulfate
options.explanation: The two products are distinct; no conversion happens between them.

check.stem: Which ion pair comes together to form the solid?

options.explanation: Lead ions and sulfate ions build the insoluble lead(II) sulfate.
Lead(II) nitrate is one of the soluble reactants, so that pair stays dissolved.
Potassium sulfate is the other soluble reactant, not the product.
That pair makes the soluble by-product, not the solid.

check.stem: In the equation Pb(NO3)2 + K2SO4 giving PbSO4 + 2KNO3, what does the 2 before KNO3 balance?

options.text: The two nitrate ions in one lead(II) nitrate unit
options.explanation: Both nitrates must reappear as two potassium nitrates on the right.

options.text: The two potassium ions in potassium sulfate
options.explanation: Those two potassiums explain why KNO3 carries a 2, but the question points at the nitrate side of the balance.
Ionic charges are already balanced inside the formulae; the 2 is a counting number.

options.text: Nothing, it is a typographical slip
options.explanation: The equation is balanced as written; the 2 is essential.

lessons.title: Method
lessons.opening: Equal volumes of the two solutions are measured, mixed and stirred, and the white solid is then collected by filtration. Washing with distilled water strips away traces of the leftover solutions, and a spell in a warm oven dries the product. Lead salts are toxic, so care is needed at every stage of the handling.
keyPoints: 25 cm3 of 0.5 mol dm-3 lead(II) nitrate solution is measured into a small beaker.
An equal volume of potassium sulfate solution is added and the mixture is stirred.
Filtration separates the precipitate from the mixture.
Distilled water washes away traces of the other solutions.
The sample is left in an oven to dry.

low.restatement: Measure 25 cm3 of each 0.5 mol dm-3 solution into a beaker and stir them together. Filter off the white solid, rinse it with distilled water, then dry it in an oven to finish the sample.
low.analogy: The method is a production line with four stations, mix, filter, wash, dry, and each station hands a cleaner product to the next.
low.examPointer: Quote the measured quantities if the question gives them, 25 cm3 of each solution, because practical write-ups expect the actual numbers.

medium.restatement: Equal volumes of equal concentrations give the ions in matching amounts, so neither reactant is left wanting when the solid forms. The wash then removes the potassium nitrate solution soaking the residue, and oven drying removes the rinse water, delivering the product dry without heating it anywhere near decomposition.
medium.analogy: Rinsing the residue before drying is like towelling off before putting on clean clothes: skip the rinse and the drying stage simply bakes the old solution onto the solid.
medium.examPointer: Safety questions expect the lead-salt toxicity named explicitly, with careful handling stated as the response.

check.stem: What volumes and concentrations are used for each solution?

options.text: 25 cm3 of 0.5 mol dm-3 for both
options.explanation: Both solutions are measured out at 25 cm3 and 0.5 mol dm-3.

options.text: 50 cm3 of 1.0 mol dm-3 for both
options.explanation: Every figure has been doubled compared with the method of record.

options.text: 25 cm3 of 0.5 mol dm-3 for lead(II) nitrate only
options.explanation: Both solutions carry the same volume and concentration in the method.

options.text: 10 cm3 of 2.0 mol dm-3 for both
options.explanation: The figures do not match the practical as written.

check.stem: After mixing, how is the solid collected?

options.explanation: Filtration is the stated collection step for the precipitate.
A burette belongs to titrations and has no role here.
Evaporation belongs to the soluble-salt method, not to collecting a precipitate.

options.text: By picking out the crystals by hand
options.explanation: That is neither safe with toxic lead salts nor a real laboratory technique here.

check.stem: The source method says to wash the filtrate. What should actually be washed, and why?

options.text: The solid residue on the filter paper, to strip away traces of the other solutions
options.explanation: The product is the residue, so it is the residue that needs the rinse.

options.text: The filtrate, because the product dissolves in it
options.explanation: The product is insoluble by design and sits above the paper, not below it.

options.text: The beaker only, since the solid is clean
options.explanation: The solid is exactly what carries the solution traces needing removal.

options.text: The filter paper before use, to wet it
options.explanation: Wetting the paper is a different technique and not what the wash step is for.
The method leaves the washed solid in an oven to dry.
Cold does not remove water; warmth does.
A naked flame is uncontrolled heating and unsuitable for a toxic salt.
Improvised equipment is not part of the method.

check.stem: What safety point applies to this practical?

options.text: Lead salts are toxic, so care is needed when handling them
options.explanation: That is the source's stated safety warning for the practical.
It is an ordinary soluble salt with no radioactivity involved.
An inorganic salt like this is not the flammable hazard; toxicity is.

options.text: No care is needed once the salt is insoluble
options.explanation: Insolubility changes nothing about the toxicity of lead compounds.

glossary.definition: The insoluble solid that separates when the two solutions are mixed.
Ions present in the mixture that take no part in forming the precipitate.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper, leaving the solid residue behind.
Purified water with no dissolved minerals, used to wash traces of other solutions off the solid.
Poisonous to the body, the reason lead salts need careful handling.
The reaction in which mixing two solutions produces an insoluble solid product.
Separating an undissolved solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through filter paper.

workedExample.prompt: A student prepares lead(II) sulfate by mixing 25 cm3 of 0.5 mol dm-3 lead(II) nitrate with 25 cm3 of 0.5 mol dm-3 potassium sulfate. a) Write the full equation with state symbols. b) Describe how the solid is collected, washed and dried. c) Why must the salt being made be insoluble for this method to work, and what safety precaution applies?
steps: b) The mixture is filtered to collect the white precipitate; the residue is washed with distilled water to remove traces of the other solutions, then left in an oven to dry.
c) The precipitate is itself the product, so the wanted salt must be insoluble while both reactants are soluble; lead salts are toxic, so they must be handled with care.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Pb(NO3)2 + K2SO4 → PbSO4 + 2KNO3. b) Filter, wash with distilled water, oven-dry. c) The precipitate is the product; lead salts are toxic — handle carefully.
